result.question:
Find and VERIFY (primary sources only, with the exact quoted sentence and page/figure/table where the number appears) the citations needed for the introduction of a concise Radiology: Artificial Intelligence paper whose thesis is: hospitals that can afford surgical navigation systems (an intraoperative wand/tracker registered to a 3-D CT/CBCT scan, e.g. Medtronic StealthStation + O-arm, Brainlab, 7D, Globus ExcelsiusGPS) localize the spinal level instrumentally, while hospitals that cannot afford them rely on manual fluoroscopic counting of vertebrae across successive C-arm shots — and a navigation system composed entirely of C-arm shots taken in the operating room would close that gap.

Answer these, each with DOI/PMID, the quoted passage, and the figure:
1. THE COUNTING PROCEDURE. Peer-reviewed descriptions of how a spine surgeon identifies/counts the vertebral level intraoperatively with a C-arm: counting up from the sacrum or down from C2/T1 on lateral and AP fluoroscopy, using the ribs / iliac crest / sacral promontory as landmarks, overlapping successive shots, marking with a needle or instrument, the difficulty in obese patients / thoracic spine / transitional anatomy; wrong-level surgery incidence and its causes (e.g., Mody 2008 "The prevalence of wrong level surgery among spine surgeons" Spine; Longo 2012; Hsu 2008 "wrong-site surgery"; Lindley 2011; Ammerman 2006 "A prospective evaluation of the role of intraoperative X-ray in lumbar disc surgery"; the JHU "LevelCheck" papers by Otake/Siewerdsen/Lo describing the manual counting workflow; Grelat 2016; Hsiang "Wrong-level surgery: a unique problem in spine surgery"). Give the ones that actually DESCRIBE the counting workflow, not just report rates.
2. THE FIDUCIAL LOCALIZATION STUDY AT A QUATERNARY CENTRE AND ITS FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS. Identify the study (or studies) where preoperative percutaneous fiducial markers (or radiologist-placed markers / methylene blue / coils) were placed to mark the target level before spine surgery at a quaternary/tertiary academic centre, with a cost or time analysis (candidates: Upadhyaya et al. 2012 J Neurosurg Spine "Prospective cost-effectiveness study of preoperative level localization with percutaneous fiducial markers" / Paolini 2005 / Binning 2010 "Percutaneous placement of radiopaque markers at the pedicle of interest for preoperative localization of thoracic spine level" / Marks 2020? / Hsu 2015?). Extract: number of patients, cost per patient, time, wrong-level rate before/after, and the exact wording of the cost conclusion.
3. NAVIGATION ACCESS DISPARITY. Verified figures for the capital cost of a navigation + intraoperative 3-D imaging system (O-arm + StealthStation, Airo, Loop-X, Excelsius) and the share of hospitals / spine surgeons with access (surveys by AO Spine, NASS, or national registries; US, Europe, LMIC; "community vs academic"). Primary sources only; flag vendor press releases.
4. Any published system that attempts level identification from C-arm shots alone without a 3-D scan (LevelCheck requires a preoperative CT; are there any that do not?), to position the contribution.
5. RSNA "Radiology: Artificial Intelligence" author instructions: current word limit, figure/table limits, structured abstract headings, required checklists (CLAIM 2024), data/code availability requirements — quote the instruction page.

Return a structured report: for each item the citation, the quoted passage, the number, and a confidence with what could not be verified.

confirmed.claim: Manbachi et al. 2018 (Introduction, paragraph 2) describes the manual intraoperative counting workflow: surgeons localize the vertebral level on intraoperative x-ray projection images (mobile radiography or C-arm fluoroscopy) by counting relative to a known landmark, counting up from the sacrum or down from C1, and this is subject to error from anatomical variants (lumbarized sacrum, thirteenth thoracic vertebra) and poor image quality. The sentence is cited to reference [6] = Hsiang J, 'Wrong-level surgery: a unique problem in spine surgery', Surg Neurol Int 2:47, 2011. The paper gives no detail on number of shots, obese patients or thoracic-specific difficulty beyond this.
confirmed.quote: Vertebral localization is often accomplished using intraoperative x-ray projection images (via mobile radiography or C-arm fluoroscopy) in which the surgeon counts vertebral levels relative to a known anatomical landmark (e.g., counting up from the sacrum or down from C1).[6] The process is subject to a variety of sources of potential error, including anatomical variations (e.g., lumbarized sacrum or thirteenth thoracic vertebra) and poor radiographic image quality.

confirmed.claim: LevelCheck requires a preoperative 3-D image (CT or MRI) as input: it solves a 6-DOF 3D-2D registration between the preoperative volume and the intraoperative radiograph (DRR matched to the radiograph via a Gradient Orientation similarity metric) and overlays the preoperatively assigned vertebral labels; it does not identify levels from C-arm shots alone. (Materials and Methods, algorithm description.)
confirmed.quote: The method, called LevelCheck, enables the vertebral labels identified in preoperative CT or MR images to be overlaid onto corresponding locations in intraoperative radiographs. ... The algorithm solves for the 3D orientation (pose) that relates a preoperative 3D image to an intraoperative 2D image—viz., a preoperative CT or MRI and an intraoperative x-ray projection image, respectively. The solution comprises 6 degrees of freedom (3 translational and 3 rotational) in orientation of the 3D preoperative image such that its projection (a digitally reconstructed radiograph, DRR) matches the 2D intraoperative radiograph.

confirmed.claim: The conventional intraoperative method for locating a vertebral level is manual 'level counting' on fluoroscopy: counting inferiorly from the occipitocervical junction for cervical/upper thoracic targets and counting up from the lumbosacral joint for lower thoracic/lumbar targets, which the authors state costs time, ionizing radiation and carries a risk of human error (attributed in-text to Hsiang 2011).
confirmed.quote: The conventional site localization method in spine surgery is level counting – i.e., counting the number of vertebrae from readily identifiable anatomical landmarks in fluoroscopy (Hsiang, 2011). For example, localizing levels in the C-spine and upper T-spine may be accomplished by first localizing the occipitocervical junction and counting inferiorly to the target level; similarly for the lower T-spine or L-spine, level localization may be accomplished by counting up from the lumbosacral joint. Such a method involves an undesirable amount of time, ionizing radiation, and risk of human error. [Introduction]

confirmed.claim: LevelCheck requires a preoperative CT: it is an intensity-based 3D-2D CT-to-fluoroscopy registration in which target levels are defined on the preoperative CT in a planning step, and the authors flag deformation between the preoperative CT and intraoperative fluoroscopy as an open consideration — so it is not a C-arm-only level-identification system.
confirmed.quote: We propose an image registration and visualization system (referred to as LevelCheck), for decision support in spine surgery by automatically labeling vertebral levels in fluoroscopy using a GPU-accelerated, intensity-based 3D-2D (viz., CT-to-fluoroscopy) registration. [Abstract] ... the target vertebral levels (and other structures or trajectories of interest as desired) are defined in a 3D volume image in a preoperative planning step. [Introduction] ... An important consideration in application of the registration method to a realistic clinical scenario is the deformations and other perturbations (e.g., introduction of surgical tools) to the patient occurring between the preoperative CT and intraoperative fluoroscopy. [Discussion]

confirmed.claim: The standard intraoperative method for preventing wrong-level spine surgery is intraoperative X-ray (C-arm) that lets the surgeon count vertebral levels one by one; the article does NOT specify the landmark (sacrum-up or C2-down) or the AP/lateral shot sequence, so it supports 'counting on fluoroscopy is the default workflow' but not the mechanics of the count.
confirmed.quote: The current method to prevent wrong-level spine surgery performed is by intra-operative X-ray which allows the surgeon to count the spine level one by one.

confirmed.claim: Computer-assisted image guidance (navigation) reduces wrong-level risk but is not available in all hospitals and is not practical for every spine operation (Hsiang cites Nowitzke et al. 2008, Spine J 8:597-604, DOI 10.1016/j.spinee.2007.06.005, as the image-guidance evidence). This is a direct peer-reviewed statement of the navigation access gap, though it gives no percentage or cost figure.
confirmed.quote: Even though computer-assisted image guidance can help to reduce the risk of wrong level surgery,[6] this technology is not readily available in all hospitals, and it is not practical to apply to all spine surgeries.

confirmed.claim: Wrong-level spine surgery prevalence among responding AANS neurosurgeons was 1 in 3110 procedures: 418 wrong-level operations out of an estimated 1,300,000 spine procedures (Abstract, Results, p. 194; verified verbatim from NCBI PubMed efetch XML and Europe PMC REST, identical wording). Full text (pp. 194-198) is paywalled at Ovid and LWW (HTTP 402) and has no open-access copy per Semantic Scholar, so the denominator's derivation and any table could not be checked.
confirmed.quote: From an estimated 1,300,000 spine procedures, 418 wrong level spine operations had been performed, with a prevalence of 1 in 3110 procedures.

confirmed.claim: Half of responding spine surgeons (207 of 415, 50%) reported having performed at least one wrong-level surgery in their career, and a further 15% (64) had prepared the wrong level and caught it before incision; the survey went to all 3505 members of the neurosurgical society with a 12% response rate, so the prevalence rests on a self-selected 415 respondents (Abstract, Methods and Results, p. 194). Note the abstract's wording 'American Academy of Neurologic Surgeons' is as published; the society is the AANS.
confirmed.quote: A total of 415 (12%) surgeons responded. Sixty-four surgeons (15%) reported that, at least once, they had prepared the incorrect spine level, but noticed the mistake before making the incision. Two hundred seven (50%) reported that they had done 1 or more wrong level surgeries during their career.

confirmed.claim: In a prospective series of 100 consecutive single-surgeon lumbar discectomies, the surgeon's anatomic identification of the exposed level (before radiographic confirmation) was correct in only 85% of cases, i.e. a 15% initial wrong-level exposure rate when the level is judged without imaging. (Verified from the PubMed/NLM abstract, PMID 17084188, DOI 10.1016/j.surneu.2006.05.069; Surg Neurol 2006 Nov;66(5):470-3.)
confirmed.quote: we examined 100 consecutive patients who underwent lumbar discectomy by a single surgeon. After exposure, the surgeon was asked to identify the level exposed, which was confirmed by intraoperative x-ray. [...] The intended level was initially exposed in 85% of cases.

confirmed.claim: Patient age and level of pathology were statistically significant predictors (P < .05) of a mismatch between the exposed level and the pathological level, with pathology above L5-S1 (i.e. levels that cannot be identified directly off the sacrum) predicting incorrect exposure.
confirmed.quote: Age and level of pathology (P < .05) were identified as factors predictive of a mismatch between intraoperative level of exposure and preoperative level of pathology. [...] Pathology above L5-S1 and patient age have been shown to reliably predict incorrect level exposure.

confirmed.claim: Under 2013 CPT coding, preoperative gold fiducial implantation for thoracic level localization costs $1,237.55 under fluoroscopic guidance and $1,267.03 under CT guidance (Macki et al. 2014, Neurol Res 36(10):925-927, DOI 10.1179/1743132814Y.0000000413, PMID 24963696; number verified verbatim in the PubMed/Europe PMC abstract; the full text at Taylor & Francis returned HTTP 403 and the article is not in PMC, so the table/page in the body could not be checked).
confirmed.quote: Following 2013 Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) coding, the cost of vertebroplasty under fluoroscopic guidance, $3195·43, or under computed tomography (CT) guidance, $3232·54, is more than double the cost of the gold fiducial implantation - $1237·55 and $1267·03, under similar imaging techniques, respectively.

confirmed.claim: The comparator preoperative marking method, percutaneous vertebroplasty with PMMA cement at the target thoracic level, costs $3,195.43 (fluoroscopy) or $3,232.54 (CT) under 2013 CPT coding, i.e. more than double the fiducial cost; the paper's stated conclusion is that the gold fiducial is 'a safe and cost-effective method for preoperative localization of the thoracic levels' (exact cost-conclusion wording).
confirmed.quote: In the first description of gold fiducials in the thoracic spine, we conclude that the marker is a safe and cost-effective method for preoperative localization of the thoracic levels.

confirmed.claim: Upadhyaya et al. (J Neurosurg Spine 2012;16(3):280-284; DOI 10.3171/2011.3.SPINE10445; PMID 22054638; Department of Neurological Surgery, UCSF; corresponding author Jau-Ching Wu, Taipei Veterans General Hospital; published online 4 Nov 2011) is a retrospective comparison of 26 thoracic-spine patients who had a CT-guided percutaneous 5-mm fiducial screw placed preoperatively (often as outpatients) against 26 HISTORICAL controls localized with intraoperative fluoroscopy alone. It is not a prospective cost-effectiveness study, and the title given in the task brief ('Prospective cost-effectiveness study of preoperative level localization with percutaneous fiducial markers') does not exist; the real title is 'Avoidance of wrong-level thoracic spine surgery: intraoperative localization with preoperative percutaneous fiducial screw placement.'
confirmed.quote: To avoid wrong-level surgery in the thoracic spine, the authors preoperatively placed a percutaneous 5-mm fiducial screw at the level of intended surgery using CT guidance. Plain radiographs and CT images with reconstructed views can then be referenced in the operating room to verify the surgical level, and the fiducial screw is easily identified on intraoperative fluoroscopy. The authors compared a group of 26 patients who underwent preoperative (often outpatient) fiducial screw placement prior to open or minimally invasive thoracic spine surgery to a historical group of 26 patients who had intraoperative localization with fluoroscopy alone. [Abstract, Methods; verbatim from NCBI efetch XML, Europe PMC and thejns.org, all identical]

refuted.claim: The paper attributes the wrong-level surgery rate to Mody et al. 2008: a survey of 3,505 physicians in which 50% of spine surgeons reported at least one wrong-level surgery in their career and wrong-level surgery occurs about once in 3,110 spine surgeries; it further attributes wrong-level errors primarily to the absence of uniquely identifiable radiographic landmarks in the mid-thoracic spine.

Preoperative CT-guided placement of radio-opaque fiducials (metallic screws per Upadhyaya et al. 2012; PMMA markers per Hsu et al. 2008) is described as the accurate alternative to counting, but one that adds time, cost, dose, infection risk and inter-departmental logistics — this identifies Upadhyaya 2012 as the fiducial-localization study for the cost/quaternary-centre argument.

unverified.claim: The study does NOT demonstrate a reduction in wrong-level surgery: the wrong-level rate was 0/26 in the fiducial group and 0/26 in the fluoroscopy-only historical cohort, and there were no fiducial-placement complications. Any introduction citing this paper as evidence that fiducials reduce wrong-level surgery would misstate it; its only positive outcome is fluoroscopy time.

The abstract gives NO numeric fluoroscopy-time figure, only 'greatly reduced'. The '3 vs 15 minutes' number that the project already cites (docs/SWEEP_TIME_EVIDENCE.md line 41) is not in any accessible part of the primary paper; it comes secondhand from the systematic review by Strong et al., J Neurosurg Spine (online 19 Nov 2021; DOI 10.3171/2021.8.SPINE21480; PMID 34798613; PMC10193475), which reads the paywalled body. The primary full text is closed access (Europe PMC 'Subscription required'; Semantic Scholar 'CLOSED'; OpenAlex oa_status 'closed', any_repository_has_fulltext False; thejns.org 'USD $45.00'), so whether 3/15 are means or medians, and whether they are beam-on seconds or wall-clock minutes, remains unverified against the primary source.

No cost, dollar, cost-per-patient, or cost-effectiveness figure appears in the abstract, and the word 'quaternary' appears nowhere in the accessible material (abstract, keywords 'thoracic spine; fiducial screw; wrong level; intraoperative localization; percutaneous', MeSH, headings). The 19-item reference list does include two cost papers (Chatterjee et al. 2011, Ann Plast Surg 66:245-248, carpal-tunnel OR-vs-clinic cost analysis; Hecht et al. 2011, Clin Orthop Relat Res 469:1035-1041, intraoperative CT cost-effectiveness), so the Discussion may argue cost qualitatively, but no cost number attributable to this paper can be verified. For the 'quaternary centre + cost' motivation, this citation should be used only for: thoracic level localization is hard; 26 vs 26; zero wrong-level in both arms; fluoroscopy time reduced; outpatient CT-guided placement adds a separate procedure.

Under 2013 CPT coding, marking a thoracic level by percutaneous vertebroplasty (PMMA) costs $3195.43 under fluoroscopic guidance or $3232.54 under CT guidance, versus $1237.55 (fluoro) and $1267.03 (CT) for gold fiducial implantation, i.e. more than double. Source: abstract (paper is 3 pages, Neurol Res 2014;36(10):925-7). Not verified: which CPT codes compose these figures; full text 403 at tandfonline.

Even the cheaper option for preoperative thoracic level localization is a separate image-guided percutaneous procedure costing roughly $1,240-$1,270 per patient (2013 CPT), which the authors present as the 'cost-effective' baseline; this is the per-patient financial burden that a C-arm-only intraoperative localization system would remove. Not verified from the abstract: patient count, procedure time, wrong-level rate before/after, and institution (affiliations absent from the MEDLINE XML; authors Bydon/Naff are commonly associated with Johns Hopkins but this is not stated in the retrieved record).

[Item 1, counting procedure] The standard intraoperative level-localization workflow is needle localization under lateral fluoroscopy, placing needles every few levels while counting cephalad from the sacrum; it depends on the surgeon knowing the patient's rib count and number of lumbar/thoracic vertebrae from preoperative imaging, and transitional anatomy or extra/missing ribs compromise it. (Strong et al., Results, 'Intraoperative Localization Techniques' section; scratch line 194 and 203; the Chin 2017 variant is ref 41, Clin Spine Surg 2017;30(1):E54-E58, DOI 10.1097/BSD.0b013e3182a35762.)

[Item 2, fiducial study] Upadhyaya et al. 2012 (ref 5; J Neurosurg Spine 2012;16(3):280-284, DOI 10.3171/2011.3.SPINE10445; UCSF, Mummaneni senior author; actual title 'Avoidance of wrong-level thoracic spine surgery: intraoperative localization with preoperative percutaneous fiducial screw placement', NOT 'Prospective cost-effectiveness study') compared CT-guided percutaneous fiducial screws in 26 patients against a historical control of needle localization counting up from the sacrum: zero wrong-level surgery in both arms, intraoperative fluoroscopy time 3 vs 15 minutes. This review reports NO per-patient cost for Upadhyaya. Cost figures the review does give, each from a different primary: coil marking procedural charge ~$1000 at one institution (ref 19, Binning & Schmidt 2010, 14 patients, 100% correct level); gold fiducials 'safe and cost-effective' vs PMMA vertebroplasty (ref 16, Macki et al. 2014 Neurol Res 36(10):925-927, Johns Hopkins); esophageal temperature probe ~$2 (ref 43); intraoperative MRI ~$2000 (ref 45). Review's own limitation: 'the costs reported are relative and not standardized'. (Scratch lines 168, 170, 176, 200-201, 210.)

[Item 3, navigation access disparity] The review states explicitly that not all hospitals have intraoperative navigation / 3-D imaging, puts the purchase cost of a navigation system at upwards of $250,000 (citing ref 39, Watkins RG et al., 'Cost-effectiveness of image-guided spine surgery', Open Orthop J 2010;4:228-233, DOI 10.2174/1874325001004010228) and the per-use cost including an intraoperative CT at approximately $7000 (citing ref 40, Costa F et al., Spine J 2014;14(8):1790-1796, DOI 10.1016/j.spinee.2013.10.019). These are secondary citations; both primaries must be checked for the exact figures (Watkins 2010 is a 2010 US figure; Costa 2014 is an Italian cost-effectiveness study of O-arm navigation in lumbar pedicle screws). No survey of the share of hospitals with access is given. (Scratch line 192.)

In a prospective single-centre series (Sant'Anna University Hospital Ferrara, Italy; April 2015 to September 2018), intraoperative localization of the target thoracic level took 3 min with a preoperatively CT-placed radiopaque fiducial versus 15 min with the standard intraoperative fluoroscopy technique. This 15 min is a direct measurement of the time cost of manual fluoroscopic level counting and is the number the RSNA-AI introduction can cite; the abstract gives NO monetary cost per patient and the study's stated aim is time and radiation dose, not cost (full text paywalled: ScienceDirect HTTP 403, Europe PMC isOpenAccess=No, hasPDF=No, so any cost statement in the Discussion is unverified).

The comparison rests on 30 patients: 19 who had a preoperative CT-guided radiopaque marker placed over the lamina or spinous process and 11 who had conventional intraoperative fluoroscopic localization. The cohort is small and non-randomised (allocation method not stated in the abstract), so the 3 vs 15 min difference carries no reported confidence interval or p-value in the abstract.
